The objection: the classification jumps from "V contains at most one positive number" to "V ⊆ {0} or V ⊆ {0,c}", without ruling out g(x) < 0 for some x. This case (negative values of g) is never treated, so the case analysis is incomplete.

Actually, how does one show $g(x) \ge 0$? One standard way: if $g(x) = -d < 0$, then $g(x - nd) = -d$ for all $n$ by iterating (4) backwards... wait, (4) says $g(x + g(x)) = g(x)$, i.e., $g(x - d) = g(x) = -d$ when $g(x) = -d$. Iterating: $g(x - nd) = -d$ for all $n \ge 0$ as long as arguments stay positive. But for large $n$, $x - nd \le 0$, contradicting... wait, but we need $g$ defined only on positive reals. Actually, $f(x - nd)$ is only defined if $x - nd > 0$. But (4) says $g(z + g(z)) = g(z)$, so starting from $x$ with $g(x) = -d$, we get $g(x - d) = -d$. This requires $x - d > 0$ for $g(x-d)$ to be defined? Hmm, actually $f$ maps $\mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, so $f$ is defined at $x - d$ only if $x - d > 0$. But wait, we need to be careful: (4) holds for all $x > 0$: $g(x + g(x)) = g(x)$. Since $f(x) = x + g(x) > 0$, the argument $x + g(x)$ is positive automatically. So applying (4) at $z = x$ gives $g(x - d) = -d$, and $x - d = f(x) > 0$... wait no. If $g(x) = -d$, then $x + g(x) = x - d = f(x) > 0$. So indeed $f(x) = x - d > 0$. Then apply (4) at $z = x - d$: $g((x-d) + g(x-d)) = g(x-d)$, i.e., $g(x - 2d) = -d$, provided $x - d > 0$ which it is, and then $x - 2d = f(x-d) > 0$. Inductively, $x - nd = f^{(n)}$-ish... actually the sequence $x, x-d, x-2d, \ldots$ are the forward iterates of $f$: $f(x) = x - d$, $f^2(x) = x - 2d$, etc. All are positive since $f$ maps positives to positives. But eventually $x - nd \le 0$ for $n > x/d$, contradiction. Hence $g(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$.

So indeed the fact $g \ge 0$ requires a (short) argument, which the objector even provides: "if $g(x_0)=-d<0$, iterating (4) gives $g(x_0-nd)=-d$ and $x_0-nd>0$ for all $n$, impossible."
